subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Prisoners Dilemma Unpacked
description: A 60-second lesson on Prisoners Dilemma Unpacked.

hook.text: Two friends are caught shoplifting. Police separate them. If both stay silent, light sentence.

buildup.text: Each prisoner reasons: if the other stays silent, I gain by confessing. If the other confesses, I must confess too.

discovery.text: The dominant strategy is to defect, but mutual cooperation beats mutual defection.

twist.text: Real humans cooperate more than theory predicts. In experiments, about 40% cooperate even in one-shot games.

climax.text: The Prisoners Dilemma appears everywhere: arms races, climate change, price wars.

punchline.text: The rational choice leads to the worst outcome for both.

quiz.question: Why do both prisoners confess even though silence is collectively better?
options: They want to punish each other
Confessing is individually rational regardless of the other's choice
They cannot understand the payoff structure

details.summary: The prisoner's dilemma is the foundational game theory scenario where two rational players both choose to defect even though mutual cooperation would benefit both, illustrating why individually rational choices can produce collectively irrational outcomes.
details.whyItMatters: The prisoner's dilemma models arms races, climate negotiations, price wars, and countless social situations where self-interest undermines collective welfare. Behavioral insights reveal how real people cooperate far more than theory predicts.
takeaways: Rational self-interest leads both players to defect despite mutual benefit from cooperation
Real humans cooperate roughly 40 to 60 percent of the time in experiments
Repeated interaction, communication, and social norms increase cooperation

faq.question: Why do real people cooperate when theory says they should not?
faq.answer: People bring social preferences like fairness, reciprocity, and altruism into strategic interactions. They also anticipate future interaction, feel guilt about betrayal, and use moral reasoning that standard game theory ignores.

faq.question: What is the most successful prisoner's dilemma strategy?
faq.answer: In Robert Axelrod's famous tournament, tit-for-tat won: cooperate first, then copy the opponent's last move. It succeeds because it is nice, retaliatory, forgiving, and transparent. Simple reciprocity outperformed complex strategies.
